title: Helper Self-Challenge
overview: Chapter 7 turns the idea of self-challenge on the helper. Egan first gives eight guidelines for making invitations to client self-challenge wise rather than merely accurate. He then distinguishes reluctance (misgivings about the hard work of change) from resistance (pushing back against perceived coercion), describes their forms and causes, and sets out unhelpful and productive ways of responding. A section on principled negotiation shows how counsellors can help clients handle conflicts with others and within themselves. The chapter ends with the shadow side of helpers: blind spots, the MUM effect and the excuses helpers make for not inviting clients to challenge themselves.
objectives: Explain why helpers need to challenge themselves and the three areas of helper self-challenge.
Describe and illustrate the eight guidelines for effective invitations to client self-challenge.
Differentiate between reluctance and resistance as defined by Egan.
Identify the forms of reluctance and its main reasons, including shame.
Explain the causes of resistance, including involuntary clients and sociocultural factors, and the idea of healthy resistance.
List unhelpful helper responses and self-defeating assumptions about reluctance and resistance.
Discuss productive approaches to helping clients move beyond reluctance and resistance.
Outline principled negotiation and its use in counselling, including negotiating with oneself.
Explain the shadow side of helpers, the MUM effect and trainees' excuses for not challenging.

sections.heading: Introduction: Helper Self-Challenge
sections.detailed:
Egan opens by turning the idea of self-challenge back on the helper. Self-challenge is not something only clients need; helpers too must keep challenging themselves to become better informed and more effective in their profession. He notes that people often ask why he keeps bringing out new editions of The Skilled Helper, a question nobody would put to authors of physics or medical texts. His answer is that every profession develops: new theories, new research and new ways of working keep appearing, even in the social sciences, so it makes little sense to take a static view of psychology and psychotherapy.

For this reason practitioners need to keep refreshing and updating their practice. Egan points out that continuing-education (CE) requirements exist across states and that a whole CE industry has grown up to meet them, which shows that ongoing learning is an accepted professional obligation.

Although helper self-challenge applies to every part of the helping process, the chapter concentrates on three areas:

1. The challenges helpers face when they invite clients to challenge themselves (building on the invitations described in Chapter 6).
2. The challenges of working with reluctant and/or resistant clients.
3. The shadow side of helpers as it relates to challenge in general.

A fourth theme, the role of negotiation in challenge, sits between the second and third areas in the chapter and shows how challenge plays out when clients are in conflict with others or with themselves. The overall message is that the quality of a helper's challenging depends heavily on how honestly the helper examines his or her own attitudes, skills and blind spots.
sections.simple: Helpers must challenge themselves just as they ask clients to. Professions keep changing, so counsellors must keep learning. The chapter looks at helper self-challenge in three areas: inviting clients to self-challenge, handling reluctance and resistance, and the helper's shadow side.
keyPoints: Self-challenge applies to helpers as much as to clients.
All professions, including psychotherapy, develop over time; practice must be updated (continuing education).
Area 1: challenges in inviting client self-challenge.
Area 2: helping reluctant and/or resistant clients.
Area 3: the shadow side of helpers in relation to challenge.

sections.heading: Guidelines for Effective Invitations to Self-Challenge
sections.detailed:
An invitation to self-challenge can be accurate, that is, on the mark, and still fail or even hurt the client. Accuracy is not enough; the invitation must also be wise. Egan says every invitation should be soaked in the relationship values discussed in Chapter 2. Specifically, invitations should be:

- Based on understanding of the client, not on the helper's favourite theories.
- Caring, not power games or put-downs.
- Genuine, not tricks or games.
- Designed to increase the client's self-responsibility, not to express helper control.
- Aimed at helping the client move into outcome-focused action, not endless discussion.

Empathy should run through every invitation. Inviting self-challenge is not a skill that comes automatically; helpers have to draw on all the communication and relationship-building skills of Part II of the book (tuning in, listening, empathic responding, probing and summarizing).

Egan then offers a set of helper self-challenge principles that act as basic guidelines for making the invitations of Chapter 6 not merely accurate but wise. There are eight guidelines: keep the goals of invitations in mind; do not force decisions but provide choice structure; earn the right to invite self-challenge; help clients be specific; be tentative but not apologetic; challenge unused strengths rather than weaknesses; help clients build on successes; and make sure invitations respect clients' values. At the end of the section Egan stresses that these are guidelines, not absolute prescriptions, and summarizes them in Box 7.1, "The Wisdom of Challenging".
sections.simple: A challenge can be correct and still do harm. Invitations should be empathic, caring, genuine, aimed at client self-responsibility and action. Egan gives eight guidelines to make invitations wise, not just accurate.
keyPoints: Invitations can be 'on the mark' yet ineffective or hurtful.
Must reflect Chapter 2 values: understanding, caring, genuineness, self-responsibility, action focus.
Empathy should permeate every invitation.
Draws on all Part II communication skills.
Eight guidelines make invitations wise, not just accurate.

sections.heading: Keep the Goals of Invitations to Client Self-Challenge in Mind
sections.detailed:
The first guideline is that invitations to self-challenge must be woven into the whole helping process rather than used as isolated interventions. Their goal is to help clients develop the alternative perspectives, internal behaviour and external actions needed to achieve the three general outcomes described in Chapter 1. Counsellors must help each client personalize these broad outcomes. Life-enhancing outcomes for the client are the bottom line of helping, but the client must discover and buy into any particular set of outcomes; they cannot simply be handed down by the helper.

Egan illustrates what goes wrong when a helper loses sight of this goal with the case of Chris, a therapist who is politically and socially very conservative. Chris tends to invite clients to challenge thinking and behaviour that clash with his own values and principles, and sometimes he goes beyond invitation to outright confrontation. With Serena, a young drug user who has moved back home, he tells her she is operating from a self-defeating philosophy, roughly "I can do anything I want, but if I get into trouble society has to look after me", and that this will keep her at odds with her parents, herself and society.

Egan's comment is that this might be acceptable in a conversation between friends, but Chris is a helper, not a friend. What he says may even be true, but forcing truth on clients usually leads nowhere. A better course would be to help Serena discover her own philosophy of life and then explore its consequences, especially the unintended ones. Chris could even admit honestly that their philosophies are so different that he may not be the best therapist for her. The key lesson: helping sessions are not the place to proselytize.
sections.simple: Challenges should serve the client's own life-enhancing goals, which the client must choose and own. The therapist Chris pushes his conservative values on Serena; Egan says helpers should help clients explore their own philosophy, not preach.
keyPoints: Integrate invitations into the whole helping process.
Aim: new perspectives, internal behaviour and external action toward the three outcomes of Chapter 1.
Clients must discover and buy into their own outcomes.
Chris and Serena: truth 'shoved down the throat' leads nowhere.
Helping sessions are not for proselytizing.

sections.heading: Don't Force Clients to Make Decisions, But Do Provide "Choice Structure"
sections.detailed:
Choice structures do not push clients into a particular decision. Instead they help clients see things in a new light and free them to make decisions they otherwise would not have made (Corsini, 2011; Hagedorn, 2011). The helper arranges the situation so that the client can discover something for himself.

Egan's example involves a father who has complained at length about his son's ingratitude. The complaining has been cathartic, but it is time to move on. The counsellor notes that people often have blind spots in close relationships and asks the father to imagine his son sitting with a counsellor talking about him: what would the son say? After hesitating, the father says the son would say he loves him but has always resented his "interference" since the mother died, because the father kept steering his life. The counsellor reflects this as love mixed with resentment of control. The father then admits the son would be right, that being pushy is part of his instinctive style, that he is starting to see its negative impact at work too, though he is unsure he will ever change.

By asking the client to "walk" a little in his son's shoes, the counsellor provided a choice structure that let the client challenge himself about the controlling, dysfunctional side of his interpersonal style and its unintended negative consequences. Egan adds wryly that not all clients respond so readily. As an alternative choice structure, the counsellor might have asked him to list three things he does right and three things he should reconsider in his relationship with his son. The general point is to be inventive in the probes and choice structures offered to clients so that they can challenge themselves.
sections.simple: Helpers should not decide for clients but can set up situations (choice structures) that help clients see things differently and choose freely. Asking a controlling father to imagine his son's view helped him see his own pushiness.
keyPoints: Choice structures help clients see things differently without forcing decisions (Corsini; Hagedorn).
Example: father asked to imagine his son talking to a counsellor about him.
Client discovered son's love mixed with resentment of his control.
Alternative: list three things done right and three to reconsider.
Be inventive with probes and choice structures.

sections.heading: Earn the Right to Invite Clients to Challenge Themselves
sections.detailed:
Long ago Berenson and Mitchell (1974) argued that some helpers do not have the right to invite clients to challenge themselves because they are not keeping their own houses in order. Egan thinks the point is worth exploring and debating because it raises the question of whether helping is a profession or a vocation. He lists four ways helpers can earn the right to challenge.

1. Develop a solid relationship. Challenge only after investing time and effort in building a relationship. If rapport is poor or the relationship has stagnated, the helper should challenge himself or herself to handle the relationship more creatively. Egan asks whether conservative Chris can relate to liberal clients.

2. Invitations should spring from empathy. Effective challenge flows from accurate understanding. Only by seeing the world through clients' eyes can a helper see how their thinking, behaving and emotional expression get them into trouble and keep them there. Empathy is not an optional extra; it should give substance to every helper response. If Chris always starts from his own worldview, he reduces his value to clients.

3. Be open to invitations to challenge yourself. Helpers who handle poorly the invitations others make to them, in sessions or in daily life, should hesitate to invite others. A helper who is defensive with clients, supervisors or in everyday life will sound hollow. Helpers should model the nondefensive attitudes they hope to see in clients. Chris, for instance, has a liberal brother; their phone calls usually end in acrimony because his liking for debate overrides his capacity for empathy.

4. Work on your own life. Berenson and Mitchell claimed that only people striving to live fully by their own value system have the right to invite others to challenge themselves, because only such people can be sources of "human nourishment" for others. Helpers might ask: why should others accept invitations from me, and what remains unchallenged in my own life?

Egan adds that even if one disagrees with Berenson and Mitchell, one must still decide what gives one the right to challenge. Avoiding all challenge avoids conflict but leaves interactions bland. He clarifies that his conservative-versus-liberal example does not favour either side; the real question in a highly diverse world of conflicting philosophies, values and ethics is how well the helper handles diversity without surrendering his or her own values.
sections.simple: Helpers must earn the right to challenge. They do this by building a good relationship, basing challenges on empathy, being open to being challenged themselves, and working on their own lives (Berenson and Mitchell).
keyPoints: Berenson and Mitchell (1974): some helpers lack the right to challenge.
Raises the question: is helping a profession or a vocation?
Four ways: solid relationship; empathy; openness to self-challenge; work on your own life.
Model nondefensive attitudes; be a source of 'human nourishment'.
Avoiding all challenge keeps interactions bland; handle diversity without surrendering your values.

sections.heading: Help Clients Be Specific in Their Self-Challenges
sections.detailed:
Specific self-challenges hit the mark; vague ones get lost because clients do not know what to do with them. A remark such as telling a client to "pull yourself together and get on with it" may meet some need of the helper, for example venting frustration, but does little for the client.

Egan gives the example of a client under heavy stress at home and work. The helper points to a specific discrepancy: the client says he wants more time with the kids and enjoys it, yet keeps accepting new assignments, such as the Eclipse project, that increase his travel. The helper suggests talking about work-life balance. The client is cynical: the company talks about balance but nothing happens, and nobody at work seems to have it right. The helper then applies a saying about careers, that if you are not in charge of your career nobody is, to work-life balance. The client realizes that responsibility sits on his own shoulders and that he has been waiting for his family and company to sort it out for him. They go on to discuss the specifics he wants in his own work-life balance "package".

Egan notes that some helpers avoid clarity and specificity because they fear being intrusive. However, helping often has to be intrusive to make a difference.
sections.simple: Vague challenges like "pull yourself together" do not help. Specific ones, such as pointing out that a stressed father keeps taking on travel-heavy projects, help clients see exactly what to change. Helping sometimes has to be intrusive.
keyPoints: Specific invitations hit the mark; vague ones get lost.
Vague statements may serve the helper's need to vent.
Example: work-life balance client and the Eclipse project.
Client realized responsibility was on his own shoulders.
Helping often has to be intrusive to make a difference.

sections.heading: Be Tentative But Not Apologetic in the Way You Invite Clients to Self-Challenge
sections.detailed:
Tentative invitations are generally viewed more positively than strong, direct challenges. Egan's principle is that when invitations are tentative, clients are more likely to respond rather than react. Invitations should be delivered as hunches that are open to review and discussion. If they sound like accusations, clients will react accordingly. Inviting self-challenge is never an opportunity to put clients in their place.

On the other hand, invitations wrapped in too many qualifications, whether in words or tone of voice, sound apologetic and are easily dismissed. Egan recalls working in a career-development centre with a client who was getting nowhere largely because he was full of self-pity. When Egan shared this, he overqualified it heavily, asking whether it had ever struck the client, in some small way, that one possible reason might be that he tended at times to engage in "a little bit of self-pity". The client stared at him and repeated, "A little bit of self-pity?" Egan feared he had been too harsh, but the client continued that he wallowed in self-pity. He had been waiting for the invitation, and they moved on to explore how he could move beyond self-pity to constructive change.

So the balance is: tentative enough to invite a response rather than defensiveness, but clear and confident enough not to be brushed aside.
sections.simple: Offer challenges as hunches so clients respond instead of getting defensive. But don't over-qualify them, or they sound weak. Egan's over-hedged "a little bit of self-pity" got the reply "I wallow in self-pity."
keyPoints: Tentative invitations are viewed more positively than strong, direct ones.
Tentative = clients respond rather than react; deliver as hunches.
Accusatory invitations provoke reactions; never 'put clients in their place'.
Over-qualified invitations sound apologetic and are easily dismissed.
Egan's self-pity client: 'I wallow in self-pity.'

sections.heading: Invite Clients to Challenge Unused Strengths Rather Than Weaknesses
sections.detailed:
Researchers in the positive psychology movement found that successful helpers tend to challenge clients' unused or underused strengths rather than their weaknesses. Egan says the movement's emphasis on strengths (Dahlsgaard, Peterson, & Seligman, 2005; Lopez, 2008; Peterson & Seligman, 2004; Wong, 2006) is just catching up with what Berenson and Mitchell said long ago. People who over-focus on failures find it hard to change. Dwelling on shortcomings leads them to belittle their achievements and withhold rewards from themselves even when they act in life-enhancing ways.

Challenging strengths means helping clients explore assets and resources they have but fail to use. In Egan's example, a counsellor meets one-to-one with Ann, a member of a self-help group at a rape crisis centre. Ann is excellent at supporting others, spotting someone in trouble and gently but forcefully inviting women who want to give up to review their decision, yet she is always down on herself. The counsellor contrasts this with how "Ann deals with Ann". Ann acknowledges she is a better giver than receiver and fears being self-indulgent. The counsellor helps her place a demand on herself to use her substantial resources in dealing with herself; since she is not self-indulgent, it is time to examine her resistance to being cared for.

Even adverse life experiences can be a source of strength. Park, Lechner, Antoni and Stanton (2009) edited a book on how medical illness can lead to positive life change. McMillen, Zuravin and Rideout (1995) studied adults' perceptions of benefit from child sexual abuse: almost half reported some benefit, such as greater knowledge of abuse, protecting other children, learning to protect themselves, and developing a strong personality, without discounting the horror of the abuse. Counsellors can therefore help clients "mine" benefits from adverse experiences, applying the old saying that good things can come from evil things. People are often more resilient than we assume.
sections.simple: Good helpers point clients toward strengths they are not using rather than harping on weaknesses. Ann helps others well but neglects herself. Even bad experiences, like illness or abuse, can produce strengths that clients can "mine".
keyPoints: Successful helpers challenge unused/underused strengths (positive psychology).
Positive psychology is catching up with Berenson and Mitchell.
Over-focus on failure makes change hard and blocks self-reward.
Ann: better giver than receiver; challenged to use her resources on herself.
Adversity can yield strengths (Park et al., 2009; McMillen et al., 1995 — almost half reported benefit).

sections.heading: Help Clients Build on Their Successes
sections.detailed:
Effective helpers do not push clients to place too many demands on themselves at once. They help clients make reasonable demands and, along the way, appreciate and celebrate their successes.

Egan's example is Anan, a Middle Eastern student who has just completed a business degree and is talking with a counsellor at the university placement centre. Anan has been an excellent student and relates very well to people, but he constantly undersells himself; after each success he brightens briefly and then slips back into an "I'm not very good" mindset. He tells the counsellor he has little experience and just needs "any job".

Counselor A asks why he keeps underselling himself, calls it treating himself like damaged goods and warns no one will hire him. Egan says this counsellor emphasizes the problem and browbeats the client.

Counselor B agrees experience matters but reframes Anan's past four years as two "jobs": being a learner and being a good relater. When Anan objects that school is not the real world, Counselor B gently questions this, and Anan admits he has learned a lot and gets on with nearly everyone. Counselor B then role-plays a recruiter asking him what kind of learner he is and how he builds relationships. Hesitantly, Anan describes loving deep understanding of fundamental concepts rather than studying for tests.

They go on to explore how Anan can use these successes as a job candidate. They also discuss his culture, which values modesty, had high unemployment and prized even lowly jobs. Anan is now a U.S. citizen, and Counselor B helps him consider the consequences of excessive modesty and develop a self-presentation that neither oversells nor undersells: does he present himself as a beggar or an asset? Belittling himself is a form of "fudging", which Anan dislikes.
sections.simple: Help clients make reasonable demands and celebrate their wins. With Anan, the browbeating counsellor fails, while the second counsellor reframes his studies and people skills as two successful "jobs" he can present honestly to employers.
keyPoints: Avoid too many demands at once; help clients celebrate successes.
Anan undersells himself despite real achievements.
Counselor A browbeats; Counselor B builds on successes.
Reframes four years as two 'jobs': learner and relater.
Culture of modesty explored; aim to neither oversell nor undersell.

sections.heading: Make Sure That Invitations to Self-Challenge Respect Clients' Values
sections.detailed:
Helpers should help clients clarify their values and make reasonable choices based on them, and be wary of using challenge, even indirectly, to make clients accept the helper's values. Doing so violates the empowerment value of Chapter 2.

Egan's example is a 21-year-old woman who has cut back her social life, education and career to care for her elderly mother, who has early Alzheimer's. She says juggling work, home and school is hard and she feels she is doing justice to none of them.

Counselor A tells her she has a right to her own life and should put her mother in a nursing facility, visit regularly and get on with life, adding that this is probably what her mother wants. Egan notes that inviting clients to clarify values is legitimate, but this counsellor does nothing to help her clarify them; she makes suggestions without finding out why the client is doing what she does.

Counselor B acknowledges she is juggling four important areas (her mother, school, work and social life) and suggests exploring what drives her and how she sets priorities. The client says she has never thought about it; she assumed people just have values and act on them. Counselor B invites her to check whether that is so. This counsellor gently challenges her to find out what she really wants. Helpers can help clients explore the consequences of their values, but inviting clients to look at their values is different from questioning them. Helpers may, however, invite clients themselves to question values that seem life-limiting rather than life-enhancing.

Egan closes the guidelines by saying they are guidelines, not absolute prescriptions. Use common sense, put yourself in the client's shoes and get the client to say what he or she needs. The more flexible the helper, the more value he or she adds. Box 7.1, "The Wisdom of Challenging", lists self-check questions: do I invite clients to challenge themselves; earn the right to do so; stay tactful and tentative without being insipid or apologetic; help clients make specific self-challenges; help them challenge strengths rather than weaknesses; make sure self-challenge does not become self-demeaning or self-destructive; and invite clients to clarify and act on their own values?
sections.simple: Challenges must help clients clarify and act on their own values, not adopt the helper's. A daughter caring for her mother is helped by exploring what drives her, not by being told to use a nursing home. Box 7.1 summarizes the wisdom of challenging.
keyPoints: Help clients clarify and act on their own values; imposing values violates empowerment.
Counselor A pushes a nursing home without understanding the client's reasons.
Counselor B explores what drives her priorities.
Looking at values is not the same as questioning them.
Guidelines are not absolute prescriptions; flexibility adds value (Box 7.1).

sections.heading: The Challenges Related to Helping Clients Manage Reluctance and Resistance
sections.detailed:
Helpers inevitably meet clients who are reluctant to do the often hard work that problem-managing change demands. They also meet clients who do not just drag their feet but push back, sometimes vigorously, against helping in general or against parts of the helping process. This pushing back is resistance.

Egan deliberately distinguishes between "reluctance" and "resistance", even though the two terms are often used interchangeably in the literature, and he notes that some clients are both reluctant and resistant.

- Reluctance (misgivings about change): its seeds are in the client. It refers to the client's hesitancy to engage in the work required by the helping process, rooted in the difficulty of change and the fact that its rewards are not always immediately visible.
- Resistance (reacting to coercion): it is the client's reaction to feeling forced, coerced or mistreated, whether by the helper, a referral source or the helping system. Resisting clients tend to think they are being made to do something.

In short, reluctance is about the work of change; resistance is about the perceived pressure to change. Reluctance is a form of avoidance; resistance is a form of fighting back. Both are pervasive, and in practice a mixture of the two is often found in the same client.
sections.simple: Reluctance means foot-dragging because change is hard work; it comes from within the client. Resistance means pushing back because the client feels forced or mistreated. Egan separates the two, though others often use them as synonyms and many clients show both.
keyPoints: Reluctance: hesitancy to do the hard work of change (seeds within the client).
Resistance: 'pushing back' against helping because of perceived coercion.
Terms often used interchangeably in the literature; Egan distinguishes them.
Some clients are both reluctant and resistant.

sections.heading: Reluctance: Misgivings About Change
sections.simple: Reluctance is a client's hesitation to do the hard work of change. It shows in avoiding help, sticking to safe topics, being overly cooperative, setting unrealistic goals or blaming others. It is normal, found in everyone, and comes in degrees.
keyPoints: Definition: hesitancy to engage in the work demanded by the helping process.
Seeds are in the client; change is hard and rewards are delayed (Karl 'talks the talk').
Early form: slowness to seek or accept help (Vogel, Wester & Larson, 2007 — six beliefs).
Covert forms: safe topics, over-cooperation, unrealistic goals, blaming, games, not coming (Tim).
Reluctance is normal and admits of degrees ('armored' against change).

sections.heading: Reasons for Reluctance
sections.detailed:
Egan says the reasons for reluctance are many and built into the human condition. He offers a sampling of six.

1. Fear of intensity. When the counsellor uses high levels of tuning in, listening, empathic highlights and probing, and the client cooperates by exploring feelings, experiences, behaviours, points of view and intentions, counselling can become intense. This intensity can make both helper and client back off. Skilled helpers know counselling is potentially intense, are prepared for it, know how to support a client unused to it, and know when to back off.

2. Lack of trust. Some clients find it very hard to trust anyone, even a very trustworthy helper, and have irrational fears of betrayal. Even with explicit confidentiality in the contract, they reveal themselves slowly. The helper needs a combination of patience, encouragement and invitations to self-challenge.

3. Fear of disorganization. Some fear self-disclosure because they feel they cannot face what they might discover. The façade they have built, however much energy it takes to prop up, seems less burdensome than exploring the unknown. Such clients often start well but retreat when overwhelmed by what problem exploration uncovers. Digging into one's inadequacies always brings some disequilibrium, disorganization and crisis, yet breakthroughs often occur at crisis points. A high degree of disorganization immobilizes the client, whereas very low disorganization often signals failure to reach core concerns. By inviting "baby steps" that do not end in disaster, counsellors help clients build confidence.

4. Shame. Shame is a much-overlooked variable (Bradshaw, 2005; Kaufman, 1989; Lynd, 1958; M. Miller; Nathanson, 1987); Dearing and Tangney (2011) edited a book examining it from many viewpoints. Shame can be an important part of disorganization and crisis. The root meaning of "to shame" is to uncover, expose, wound, which suggests painful self-exploration. Shame is not only exposure to another; it is primarily exposure of self to oneself, where sensitive, vulnerable aspects of the self are revealed to one's own eyes. It is often sudden: in a flash the client sees unrecognized inadequacies before being ready. External incidents, like a casual remark, can trigger it only if, deep down, the person was already ashamed. A shame experience can be defined as an acute emotional awareness of a failure to be in some way. Farber and Sohn (2007) note shame blocks frank discussion of sexuality, which they describe as the least disclosed theme in psychotherapy and the second least discussed item within marriage. Shame also features in substance abuse (Potter-Efron, 2011) and PTSD (Herman, 2011). Laura realized Karl felt deeply ashamed of letting down his comrades, the army and his country; he covered it with bravado and felt strangely relieved at an honourable discharge because he felt he "deserved" it. Diversity complicates matters: findings on one population do not automatically transfer to another (Furukowa & Hunt, 2011). Some people share intimate details without shame, while some more conservative cultures abhor discussing intimate issues.

5. The cost of change. Some people avoid taking stock because they sense, perhaps subconsciously, that they would then have to change: give up comfortable but unproductive patterns, work harder, suffer loss, learn new skills. A couple may sense that counselling will force them to reveal themselves and then endure the agony of changing how they relate. Some clients expect counselling to be magic and are put off when change proves hard. Counsellors must help them see the outcomes are worth the effort, like the ex-smoker who, after years, said she loved her new freedom and wondered why she had waited so long.

6. A loss of hope. Some clients think change is impossible, so why try. A man in his 60s in a counselling group, brutally treated by his father, had run from hope all his life and suffered constant anxiety. Challenged by the helper and fellow group members, he rediscovered hope and with it self-responsibility, no longer focusing on the scars inflicted by his father or the self-inflicted scars of an irresponsible life. He found hope in community.

Egan stresses this is only a sampling; each of us can add to the list by looking at our own struggles with growth.
sections.simple: People resist the work of change for human reasons: fear of intense feelings, lack of trust, fear of falling apart, shame, the cost of changing, and loss of hope. Helpers should expect these and respond with support, patience and small steps.
keyPoints: Fear of intensity: deep exploration can make helper and client back off.
Lack of trust: irrational fear of betrayal; needs patience and encouragement.
Fear of disorganization: façade preferred; use 'baby steps'; too much or too little disorganization is unhelpful.
Shame: 'to uncover, expose, wound'; acute awareness of a failure to be (Farber & Sohn on sexuality).
Cost of change and loss of hope (man in his 60s found hope in community).

sections.heading: Resistance: Reacting to Coercion
sections.detailed:
Clients who resist tend to think they are being forced to do something. They may even want to engage in therapy or a particular exercise, but feel the helper is demanding rather than inviting participation. When Laura suggested using feedback surveys, Karl refused because he thought she was telling him what to do; he later said it felt like "Be a good boy and fill these surveys out for me". Laura had no intention of imposing the surveys and knew there were other collaborative ways to bring feedback into the process. The point is that resistance is triggered by perceived coercion.

Reacting to perceived mistreatment. Clients who feel mistreated by helpers tend to resist, as do clients who feel their cultural beliefs, values and norms (group or personal) are being violated. Resistance is the client's way of fighting back (Dimond et al., 1978; Driscoll, 1984). Spouses forced into marriage counselling often resist because they resent what they see as a power play. Tony becomes angry when his wife suggests he join her sessions; knowing she discussed it with her mother, he feels targeted by a conspiracy and is determined "they're not going to get me". Some clients see coercion where none exists, but because people act on their perceptions, the result is still covert or open fighting back.

Forms of resistance. Resistant clients, feeling abused, let everyone know they do not need help, show little willingness to form a working relationship, and often try to con counsellors. They are often resentful, actively try to sabotage the helping process, or end it prematurely. They can be testy or even abusive and belligerent. Resistance is a matter of degree, and not all resistant clients show extreme behaviour.
sections.simple: Resistance happens when clients feel pushed, coerced or mistreated, even if they would otherwise be willing. It is a way of fighting back and can show as hostility, conning, sabotage or quitting early. Perception matters more than the helper's intention.
keyPoints: Resisting clients feel forced; they perceive demands rather than invitations (Karl and the surveys).
Reaction to perceived mistreatment or violation of cultural values; a way of fighting back (Dimond et al.; Driscoll).

sections.heading: Involuntary Clients and Other Sources of Resistance
sections.simple: Mandated (involuntary) clients often resist, but so can anyone who feels coerced: those who resent referrers, fear the unknown, distrust helpers, see help as weakness, need power, or differ greatly from the helper. Cultural factors like gender, race and religion also matter.

Found in schools, corrections, court-mandated marriage counselling, welfare and employment agencies.

sections.heading: Healthy Resistance
sections.detailed:
Resistance is not always negative. It can be a healthy sign, meaning clients are standing up for their rights and fighting back. Koenig (2011), writing about patients who resist doctors' recommendations, makes a point Egan applies equally to therapy clients: resistance creates an opportunity for collaborative decision making. Through resisting a recommendation, patients negotiate and collaboratively co-construct what counts as acceptable. In other words, through resistance clients become agents, negotiating or fighting for what they need.

Egan adds that in practice a mixture of reluctance and resistance is often found in the same client. If therapy is to become more efficient, counsellors must find ways to help clients deal with reluctance and resistance as quickly as possible.
sections.simple: Resistance can be healthy: clients may be standing up for their rights. Koenig shows it can lead to joint decision making. Many clients show both reluctance and resistance, and helpers should address them efficiently.
keyPoints: Resistance can be healthy: standing up for one's rights.
Koenig (2011): resistance enables collaborative co-construction of recommendations.
Through resistance clients become agents.
Reluctance and resistance often mixed in one client.
Efficient therapy requires dealing with them expeditiously.

sections.heading: Avoid Unhelpful Responses to Reluctance and Resistance
sections.simple: When clients don't cooperate, helpers can panic, placate, get hostile, give up or start power struggles. These "fight or flight" reactions often come from unrealistic beliefs like "every client must like me" or "I must succeed with everyone".
keyPoints: Managing reluctance/resistance is part of all helping (Kottler, 1992).
Beginners feel confusion, panic, irritation, guilt, hurt, rejection.
Ten unhelpful responses: placating, hostility, doing nothing, love-bombing, power struggles, scapegoating, giving up, etc.
'Fight or flight' reactions to stress.

sections.heading: Develop Productive Approaches to Dealing with Reluctance and Resistance (I): Attitudes and Self-Examination
sections.detailed:
Egan says it is impossible to identify every form of reluctance and resistance, let alone a strategy for each, so he offers principles and a general approach. The first group of principles focuses on the helper's own stance.

1. Explore your own reluctance and resistance. Examine how you react when you feel coerced or unfairly treated, and how you run away from personal growth. Helpers in touch with their own reluctance and resistance, and finding ways to overcome them, are more likely to help clients with theirs.

2. See some reluctance and resistance as normal. Help clients see that their reluctance and resistance are not "bad" or odd, since the helper's own are not. Help them see the positive side of resistance: it may show they have fibre and may be a sign of self-affirmation.

3. Accept and work with the client's reluctance and resistance. Teyber (2005) speaks of "honoring" the client's resistance, which Egan calls a central principle. Start with the client's frame of reference. Accept both the client and the reluctance or resistance; do not ignore it or be intimidated. Tell clients how you experience it and explore it with them. Model openness to challenge and be willing to explore your own negative feelings. The skill of direct, mutual talk, called immediacy (Chapter 10), is very important here. Help clients work through the associated emotions, avoid moralizing, and "befriend" the reluctance or resistance rather than meeting it with hostility or defensiveness.

4. See reluctance as avoidance. Reluctance is a form of avoidance not necessarily tied to client ill will. Helpers should understand the principles and mechanisms of avoidance behaviour discussed in texts on principles of behaviour (Watson & Tharp, 2007). Some clients avoid counselling or engage half-heartedly because they see it as lacking suitable rewards or even as punishing. Then counsellors must help them find suitable incentives. Constructive change is usually more rewarding than a miserable status quo, but clients may not see it that way at first. Present helping as rewarding and talk about outcomes.

5. Examine the quality of your interventions. Without a guilt trip, look at your own behaviour: what might seem unfair, how might the client feel coerced (you may have become too directive without realizing)? Take stock of emotions welling up when clients lash back or drag their feet and how they "leak out". Own these feelings rather than deny them. Do not overpersonalize; letting a hostile client get under your skin reduces effectiveness. The client may be resisting not because of you but because of pressure from others, yet you take the brunt; find out if you can.

6. Be realistic and flexible. There are limits to what a helper can do; know your personal and professional limits. If your expectations for change exceed the client's, the relationship can become adversarial. Rigid expectations of client and self are self-defeating.
sections.simple: Helpers should look at their own resistance, treat client resistance as normal, accept and "honor" it, understand reluctance as avoidance that needs incentives, check whether their own behaviour feels coercive, and keep expectations realistic.
keyPoints: Explore your own reluctance and resistance.
See some reluctance and resistance as normal — even a sign of fibre and self-affirmation.
Accept and work with it; 'honor' resistance (Teyber, 2005); use immediacy; befriend it; avoid moralizing.
See reluctance as avoidance (Watson & Tharp, 2007); find incentives; talk about outcomes.
Examine your interventions; don't overpersonalize; be realistic and flexible.

sections.heading: Develop Productive Approaches to Dealing with Reluctance and Resistance (II): Mutuality, Incentives and Other Helpers
sections.detailed:
The second group of principles focuses on building collaboration and widening the client's sources of help.

7. Establish a "just society" with your client. Deal with the client's feelings of coercion by providing what Smaby and Tamminen (1979) called a "two-person just society". A just society rests on mutual respect and shared planning. Establish as much mutuality as is consistent with helping goals: invite participation, involve clients in every step and all decision making, share expectations, discuss helping procedures and get reactions, and explore the helping contract with clients so they contribute to it.

8. Help the client search for incentives for moving beyond resistance. Use client self-interest to identify incentives and brainstorming to discover possible ones. For instance, realizing that he or she will remain in charge of his or her own life may be a powerful incentive.

9. Do not see yourself as the only helper in your client's life. Engage significant others such as peers and family members in helping the client face reluctance and resistance. Lawyers in Alcoholics Anonymous, for example, may handle a fellow lawyer's reluctance to enter treatment better than the counsellor can.

10. Employ reluctant and resistant clients as helpers. Where possible, put such clients in situations where they help others; the change of perspective helps them face their own unwillingness. One tactic is role reversal: the helper plays the client, showing the same reluctance or resistance, and the client takes the counsellor role to overcome it. In one case, an active AA member took a resistant alcoholic on his city rounds of hospitals, nursing homes, jails, flophouses and the streets; the alcoholic saw through other alcoholics' lame excuses and joined AA after a week. Clients can also become helpers in group counselling.

Hanna, Hanna and Keys (1999; see also Hanna, 2002; Sommers-Flanagan & Sommers-Flanagan, 2006) compiled 50 strategies, some original and many from the literature, for counselling defiant, aggressive adolescents. Many apply more widely to reluctant and resistant clients of all ages. They group the strategies into three categories: reaching clients, accepting them, and relating to them. Egan notes these describe what helpers should do anyway, but the lists are excellent reminders.
sections.simple: Helpers should build an equal, respectful partnership ("two-person just society"), help clients find personal incentives, involve family and peers, and sometimes let resistant clients help others, which changes their perspective.
keyPoints: 'Two-person just society' (Smaby & Tamminen, 1979): mutual respect and shared planning.

sections.heading: Responding to Defensive Reactions and the Notion of "Difficult" Clients
sections.detailed:
Reluctance and resistance challenge both clients and helpers, and helping clients overcome or come to terms with unwillingness is often at the heart of helping. Helpers should not be surprised when clients react strongly to invitations to self-challenge. If clients react rather than respond, the helper must help them work through their emotion-laden reluctance and resistance; if they "clam up", the helper should try to find out what is happening inside.

In Egan's example, the helper has summarized the problem situation, gently pointing out some self-destructive behaviours, and asks how it sounds. The client retorts that he thought she was on his side, she now sounds like everyone else, and he is paying her to talk like this. Though the invitation was tentative and based on what the client himself had said, he reacted defensively.

Helper A responds defensively and judicially: all I did was summarize what you said, you know you are doing yourself in, let's go through each point. He is about to assemble the evidence, which would probably lead to argument rather than dialogue. Helper B backs off: she reflects that she sounds harsh and unfair, like she is dumping on him, and suggests backing up. She does not say her summary was wrong; she gives the client space and time to think and looks for a way into constructive dialogue with the angry client.

Some call reluctant or resistant clients, or those slow to tap their resilience, "difficult" clients, and there is a tendency to treat them as bad clients. Egan says they are simply clients. Wessler, Hankin and Stern (2001) argue that "difficult client" is too one-sided because the therapist is often part of the difficulty: calling a client difficult really means the therapist is having difficulty due to his or her own emotional issues or inexperience, and should signal a need for personal and interpersonal growth. Egan agrees, but adds that clients come for help precisely because they are not managing part of their lives well, and their behaviour in sessions often illustrates poor self-management.

It is impossible to help people for long without meeting reluctance and resistance. The literature is scattered (Brodsky, 2011; McKay, Abramowitz, & Taylor, 2010; Rasmussen, 2002; Westra, 2004; Westra et al., 2011), including on the Internet (Mitchell, 2006), and some findings conflict. Helpers must use the values of Part I and the skills of Part II to help clients who, at first sight, do not want to be helped.
sections.simple: When clients react defensively, helpers should back off and give space (Helper B) rather than argue the case (Helper A). "Difficult" clients are just clients; often the helper is part of the difficulty (Wessler, Hankin and Stern).
keyPoints: Expect strong reactions; help clients work through emotion-laden resistance.
Helper A: defensive, judicial 'assemble the evidence' approach leads to argument.
Helper B: backs off without retracting, gives space, seeks dialogue.
Wessler, Hankin & Stern (2001): 'difficult client' is one-sided; therapist is often part of the difficulty.
Use Part I values and Part II skills with clients who seem not to want help.

sections.heading: The Role of Negotiation in Challenge
sections.detailed:
Egan asks what comes to mind when we hear the word "negotiation". Some think of political dialogue, as in Zimbabwe, where one side holds power and will not give it up while the duly elected side wants to exercise its right to govern, and someone steps in to help them negotiate. Others think of Company A wanting to buy Company B, with consultants often called in. Closer to home, homeowners facing foreclosure negotiate with lenders, asking what realistic deal, fair to both sides, can be worked out.

All of these are examples of what Egan calls special-event negotiation. But there is also negotiation that is part of the give-and-take of everyday life, and most of us negotiate more than we realize: who picks up the kids, how to divide household tasks, where to eat, whether to buy a new refrigerator, how to manage finances, what to do about an offensive neighbour or a son who has gone off the rails, how to handle differences in religious observance. Generally, working out arrangements with others calls for some negotiation, and we negotiate in all social settings: home, community, work, church and health care.

The link to challenge is that challenge often occurs in a context of differing interests, whether between helper and client (as in resistance) or between clients and the people in their lives. Negotiation provides a fair way of working through such differences.
sections.simple: Negotiation is not just for big events like politics, company takeovers or foreclosures; we negotiate all the time in daily life, about chores, money, family and neighbours. Egan distinguishes special-event negotiation from everyday negotiation.
keyPoints: Special-event negotiation: politics (Zimbabwe), company mergers, foreclosure.
Central question: what realistic deal is fair to both sides?
Everyday negotiation: chores, kids, finances, neighbours, religious observance.
We negotiate in all social settings more than we realize.

sections.heading: Negotiation in Counseling
sections.detailed:
Helping involves planning (developed in Part III), and planning that involves or affects others often requires negotiation. When the people involved or affected are in conflict, negotiation becomes even more important. Moreover, clients' problem situations often centre on conflicts with others; conflict is at the heart of marriage counselling and family therapy.

Egan uses the case of Mara, whose wish to create a more fulfilling future has led to conflict with her parents, especially her father. The benefits of effective negotiation are clear, but the ability to negotiate well is a life skill people pick up by chance: some become reasonably good at it, many do not. In her failed conversation with her father, Mara did not see herself as a negotiator, and her father was not open to negotiation.

Counsellors can therefore help clients negotiate fairly in conflict situations and become better negotiators in daily life. This is a natural extension of challenge: helping clients challenge themselves to approach conflicts in a principled, fair way rather than through rigid demands or withdrawal.
sections.simple: Counselling often involves conflicts with others, so negotiation matters. Most people never learn to negotiate well. Mara failed in her talk with her father; counsellors can teach clients to negotiate fairly.
keyPoints: Planning that affects others often requires negotiation.
Conflict is central to marriage and family therapy.
Negotiation skill is usually picked up by chance.

sections.heading: A Beginners' Framework: Principled Negotiation
sections.detailed:
Fisher, Ury and Patton (1991) provide a basic framework for what they call "principled" negotiation. Much popular negotiation literature focuses on "winning" and getting your own way; principled negotiation instead stresses fairness. Egan applies its rules to Mara and her father.

1. Avoid rigid bargaining positions as the starting point. Anxious, Mara blurted out what she could do for her father's business and the role she would need. Her father heard a rigid position that seemed an affront to all he had built, rejected it out of hand and called her "ungrateful". Mara, with some justification, felt rejected as a person.

2. Separate the people from the issue. Principled negotiation is mainly about the issues, problems or concerns, not the relationship between the parties. Both Mara and her father left feeling attacked; his remarks showed he thought she was negotiating about the relationship, and he struck back.

3. Focus on interests rather than positions. Mara would have done better to raise her interests (a more engaging career and later a more engaging social life) and link them to her father's. She thought talking about the dealership showed concern for his interests, but he did not hear it that way. Parties should describe their interests clearly and non-threateningly, and ideally help each other explore interests and show they understand them.

4. Search for options or solutions based on mutual interests. Solutions built on a convergence of interests let both parties buy in. Mara assumed such a convergence without really understanding her father's interests, partly because he plays his cards close to his chest.

5. Settle on an agreement that has some objectivity to it. In some negotiations objective criteria are readily available; in a house sale, the market and local sales give elastic but objective criteria, so a fair price may be a range. In Mara's case objective criteria look different: the same words from a son might have sounded more reasonable to her father, or a lender might have asked how he would strengthen management, in which case Mara's ideas from a manager might have secured the loan.

These are the bare bones; fleshed out, they help people negotiate fairly or, for counsellors, act as catalysts in clients' negotiations. The authors also advise on negotiating with a powerful counterparty, with people who refuse to negotiate, and with "dirty tricks". Ury (1991, 2007) has written on principled negotiation in difficult situations, and Fisher and Shapiro (2005) on managing emotions so they serve negotiation. Ury's "getting past no" principles that could help Mara: stay in control under pressure; defuse hostility and anger, yours and theirs; find the other person's real rather than stated interests; cope with unfair tactics; look for incentives that bring the other party back to the table and keep them there; and search for agreements meeting mutual needs and interests.

Good negotiators, and counsellors helping clients negotiate, need all the communication skills of Chapters 3 to 6. Without them, and the relationships they build, principled negotiation is impossible. Good will is essential but not enough.
sections.simple: Fisher, Ury and Patton's principled negotiation stresses fairness, not winning: avoid rigid positions, separate people from issues, focus on interests, seek mutually beneficial options, and use objective criteria. Mara broke most of these rules with her father.
keyPoints: Principled negotiation (Fisher, Ury & Patton, 1991) values fairness over winning.

sections.heading: Helping Clients Negotiate with Themselves
sections.detailed:
Counsellors can also adapt the principles of principled negotiation, including Ury's getting-past-no principles, to help clients negotiate with themselves. Some of Mara's conflicts are internal, though they have external consequences.

Because of her bi- or tri-cultural background, there are in a sense two or three Maras:
1. The Mara who culturally leans toward the beliefs, values and norms of an Iranian family with prerevolution roots.
2. The Mara who met a different Iranian culture, in some ways freer and more socially interactive, during her visit to Iran.
3. The Mara born, raised and educated in the United States, who has experienced its culture but not fully bought into it.

Carlos, her counsellor, can help her negotiate among these parts of herself as she searches for a different future. Possibly painful trade-offs lie ahead as Mara constructs a future consistent with her key beliefs and values. Internal negotiation thus applies the same ideas of interests, options and fair agreements to conflicting parts of the self.
sections.simple: Negotiation principles also work inside a person. Mara has two or three cultural "selves" (traditional Iranian, modern Iranian, American), and her counsellor Carlos can help her negotiate among them to build her future.
keyPoints: Negotiation principles can be applied to internal conflicts.
Mara's bi-/tri-cultural background creates two or three 'Maras'.

sections.heading: The Shadow Side of Helpers
sections.detailed:
Egan points to an interesting literature on the humanity and flaws of helpers (Kottler, 2010) that helps beginners, because prevention is better than cure, and experienced helpers, because old dogs can learn new tricks. Kottler offers trainees and novices an upbeat picture of what passion and commitment in the helping professions should look like.

A critical responsibility of supervisors is to help counsellors identify their blind spots and learn from them. After training, skilled helpers continue this through various forums, especially with difficult cases. They take counsel with themselves ("What am I missing here?") and with colleagues. Without becoming self-obsessed, they scrutinize and challenge themselves and their role in the relationship. Put simply, they keep learning throughout their careers about themselves, their clients and their profession. One way to identify and address one's blind spots is to elicit clear, honest feedback from clients.

The two shadow-side issues Egan examines specifically in relation to challenge are the MUM effect and the excuses helpers make for not inviting clients to challenge themselves.
sections.simple: Helpers have flaws and blind spots too (Kottler). Supervisors help trainees find them; later, helpers keep checking themselves, consulting colleagues and asking clients for honest feedback.
keyPoints: Literature on helpers' humanity and flaws (Kottler, 2010).
Supervisors help counsellors identify blind spots.
Skilled helpers ask 'What am I missing here?' and consult colleagues.
Lifelong learning about self, clients and profession.

sections.heading: The "MUM Effect"
sections.detailed:
Some counsellor trainees are initially quite reluctant to help clients challenge themselves. They fall victim to the "MUM effect": the tendency to keep mum about undesirable messages and withhold bad news even when it is in the other person's interest to hear it (Rosen & Tesser, 1970, 1971; Tesser & Rosen, 1972; Tesser, Rosen, & Batchelor, 1972; Tesser, Rosen, & Tesser, 1971).

Egan offers a historical illustration: in ancient times the bearer of bad news to the king was sometimes killed, which understandably made messengers reluctant to deliver such news. Bad news, and by extension the "bad news" in invitations to self-challenge, often stirs negative feelings in the challenger, regardless of how the challenger expects the receiver to react.

The key implication is that a helper who is comfortable with the supportive side of helping but uncomfortable with helping as a social-influence process may fall victim to the MUM effect and become less effective than he or she could be. Box 7.2 accordingly asks helpers whether they have developed the assertiveness needed to overcome it.
sections.simple: The MUM effect is the tendency to keep quiet about bad news even when the other person needs to hear it. Trainees who like being supportive but dislike influencing clients may avoid challenging and become less effective.
keyPoints: MUM effect: tendency to 'keep mum' about undesirable messages (Rosen & Tesser).
Withholding bad news even when it is in the other's interest.
Ancient bearers of bad news to kings were sometimes killed.

sections.heading: Excuses for Not Inviting Clients to Challenge Themselves
sections.detailed:
Egan considers reluctance to challenge a reasonable starting position, in his estimation far better than being too eager to challenge. However, all helping, even the most client-centred, involves social influence. Helpers need to understand their reluctance (or eagerness) to challenge, that is, to challenge themselves about challenging and about helping as a social-influence process.

When trainees examine their feelings about inviting others to self-challenge, they uncover unexplored assumptions such as:
1. I am not used to challenging others; my style is live-and-let-live and I have misgivings about intruding into people's lives.
2. If I challenge others, I open myself to being challenged; I may be hurt or learn things about myself I would rather not know.
3. I might discover I like challenging others, the floodgates will open and my negative feelings will pour out; I fear that deep down I am an angry person.
4. I am afraid I will hurt or damage others; I have seen people hurt by heavy-handed confrontations.
5. I am afraid I will delve too deeply and find problems I cannot help with, and the process will get out of hand.
6. If I challenge others, they will no longer like me, and I want my clients to like me.

Traces of these assumptions can persist long after trainees move into the field. People in many people-oriented occupations, including human-service workers and managers, are troubled by the MUM effect and invent their own excuses for not giving feedback. Being willing to invite others to challenge themselves responsibly is one thing; having the skills and wisdom to do it is another.

Box 7.2, "The Shadow Side: Self-Challenge for Helpers", asks how well the helper can: identify the games clients try to play without becoming cynical; become comfortable with the social-influence dimension and the "intrusiveness" of helping; incorporate invitations to self-challenge into one's style without becoming a confrontation specialist; develop the assertiveness needed to overcome the MUM effect; challenge the excuses one gives oneself for not inviting self-challenge; and come to grips with one's own imperfections and blind spots, both as a helper and as a "private citizen".
