practice.answer: The MUM effect is the tendency to keep mum about undesirable messages, that is, to withhold bad news even when hearing it is in the other person's interest (Rosen & Tesser). Counsellor trainees who are comfortable with support but uneasy about helping as social influence may avoid inviting clients to challenge themselves because of it, and so become less effective.

A choice structure is a probe or arrangement the helper offers that helps clients see their situation in a new light and freely make decisions they otherwise would not have made, without forcing any decision (Corsini; Hagedorn). For example, asking a controlling father to imagine his son describing him to a counsellor helped him recognize his own pushy style.

Smaby and Tamminen's term for a helping relationship built on mutual respect and shared planning. Egan uses it to counter clients' feelings of coercion: the helper invites participation, shares expectations, discusses procedures and lets clients contribute to the helping contract and all decisions.

practice.q: What does Egan mean by 'healthy resistance'?
practice.answer: Resistance can be a healthy sign that clients are standing up for their rights and fighting back. Koenig (2011) shows that by resisting recommendations, people negotiate and co-construct what is acceptable, so through resistance clients become agents fighting for what they need.

Egan deliberately separates two terms that the literature often uses interchangeably, noting that some clients show both.

Reluctance means misgivings about change. Its seeds lie in the client. It is defined as hesitancy to engage in the work demanded by the tasks of the helping process. Because problem management and opportunity development are hard and rewards are delayed, reluctance exists in all clients and all human beings. It is often covert: talking only about safe issues, seeming unsure of goals, being overly cooperative (benign sabotage), setting unrealistic goals, blaming others, playing games or not coming at all. Its reasons include fear of intensity, lack of trust, fear of disorganization, shame, the cost of change and loss of hope. Egan treats it as a form of avoidance not tied to ill will.

Resistance means reacting to coercion. Resisting clients feel forced, mistreated or that their values are violated, and they push back against helping or parts of it. It is a way of fighting back (Dimond et al.; Driscoll). It shows as denying the need for help, refusing a working relationship, conning, resentment, sabotage, premature termination or belligerence. It is common among involuntary (mandated) clients but anyone who feels coerced can resist. Unlike reluctance, it can also be healthy, a sign of clients asserting their rights (Koenig).

In short, reluctance is foot-dragging about the work of change; resistance is pushing back against perceived pressure. Both are matters of degree and often appear together.

practice.q: Explain the reasons for client reluctance described by Egan.
practice.answer:
Egan says reluctance is built into the human condition and offers six sample reasons.

1. Fear of intensity: high levels of listening, empathy and probing make counselling intense, so client and helper may back off. Skilled helpers expect this and know how to support the client and when to back off.
2. Lack of trust: some clients irrationally fear betrayal even with confidentiality; helpers need patience, encouragement and invitations to self-challenge.
3. Fear of disorganization: clients fear what self-exploration will reveal and prefer their façade. Some disorganization accompanies growth, but too much immobilizes and too little suggests core concerns are missed; "baby steps" build confidence.
4. Shame: an exposure of self to oneself, an acute emotional awareness of a failure to be. It blocks disclosure about sexuality (Farber & Sohn) and is common in substance abuse and PTSD, as with Karl. Cultural differences matter.
5. The cost of change: clients sense they will have to give up comfortable patterns, work harder and suffer loss; some expect counselling to be magic.
6. Loss of hope: the belief that change is impossible, illustrated by a man in his 60s who rediscovered hope in a counselling group.

Egan adds that this is only a sampling; helpers can extend it by reflecting on their own struggles to grow.

practice.q: What unhelpful responses and self-defeating assumptions do helpers show when faced with reluctance and resistance?
practice.answer:
Beginning helpers, unaware of how pervasive reluctance and resistance are, often feel confusion, panic, irritation, hostility, guilt, hurt, rejection or depression with uncooperative clients and then respond unhelpfully. They may accept guilt and placate the client; become impatient and hostile; do nothing and hope it disappears; proceed half-heartedly; become warmer to win the client by love; blame the client and enter a power struggle; allow themselves to be scapegoated; lower expectations of counselling; hand direction to the client; or simply give up. Egan calls these self-defeating "fight or flight" reactions to stress.

The stress also comes from the helper's own unspoken assumptions: all clients should be self-referred and committed; every client must like and trust me; I am a consultant, not a social influencer, so I should not place demands; every unwilling client can be helped; no unwilling client can be helped; I alone am responsible for the client; I must succeed completely with every client.

These beliefs are never voiced but "loiter in the background", adding to the helper's stress. Some are contradictory (every versus no unwilling client can be helped), which shows how unrealistic they are. The belief that a helper is only a consultant, not a social influencer, also links to the MUM effect discussed later in the chapter.

Egan concludes that effective helpers neither court reluctance and resistance nor are surprised by them; instead they examine their own attitudes and respond with acceptance and realism.

practice.q: Explain the principles of principled negotiation and their relevance to counselling.
practice.answer:
Counselling often involves planning that affects others and conflicts with others, central in marriage and family therapy, yet most people pick up negotiation skills by chance. Counsellors can help clients negotiate fairly.

Fisher, Ury and Patton (1991) propose principled negotiation, which values fairness over winning. Its rules, applied to Mara and her father: (1) avoid rigid bargaining positions as the starting point, since Mara's blurted plan sounded like an affront; (2) separate the people from the issue, as both felt personally attacked; (3) focus on interests rather than positions, describing them clearly and non-threateningly and helping the other explore theirs; (4) search for options based on mutual interests so both can buy in; (5) settle on an agreement with some objectivity, like market prices in a house sale.

Ury's getting-past-no principles add: stay in control, defuse hostility, find real interests, cope with unfair tactics, use incentives to keep the other at the table and seek mutual agreements. The same principles can help clients negotiate with themselves, as with Mara's two or three cultural selves. Communication skills from Chapters 3 to 6 are essential; good will alone is not enough.

Egan distinguishes special-event negotiation (political settlements, mergers, foreclosures) from the everyday negotiation of household tasks, finances and family differences, reminding helpers that clients negotiate constantly. The counsellor acts as a catalyst, helping clients approach such conflicts fairly rather than trying to "win".

practice.q: Discuss Egan's guidelines for making effective invitations to client self-challenge.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Egan argues that self-challenge applies to helpers as much as to clients. A helper's invitation can be accurate yet ineffective or hurtful, so invitations must also be wise. They should reflect the relationship values of understanding (not favourite theories), caring (not put-downs), genuineness (not tricks), increasing client self-responsibility (not helper control) and moving toward outcome-focused action. Empathy should permeate every invitation. Egan offers eight guidelines.

1. Keep the goals in mind. Invitations are integrated into the whole process and aim at new perspectives, internal behaviour and external action leading to life-enhancing outcomes that clients themselves discover and own. The therapist Chris, who confronts Serena with his conservative judgement of her "self-defeating philosophy", shows the danger; helping sessions are not for proselytizing.

2. Don't force decisions, but provide choice structure. Choice structures help clients see things differently and decide freely. Asking a controlling father to imagine his son describing him led him to recognize his pushy style. Helpers should be inventive with such probes.

3. Earn the right to challenge. Following Berenson and Mitchell, helpers earn this by building a solid relationship, basing challenges on empathy, being open to challenge themselves and modelling non-defensiveness, and working on their own lives so they can offer "human nourishment". Avoiding all challenge keeps sessions bland.

4. Help clients be specific. Vague advice like "pull yourself together" is lost; specific observations, such as a father taking on travel-heavy projects while wanting family time, hit the mark. Helping often has to be intrusive.

5. Be tentative but not apologetic. Hunches open to discussion lead clients to respond rather than react, while accusations provoke reaction. But over-qualified invitations sound weak, as when Egan's hedged mention of "a little bit of self-pity" drew the reply "I wallow in self-pity."

6. Challenge unused strengths rather than weaknesses. Positive psychology confirms what Berenson and Mitchell said: over-focus on failure blocks change. Ann, a supportive group member who neglects herself, is invited to use her resources on herself. Even adversity can yield benefits, as McMillen and colleagues found with almost half of adult abuse survivors.

7. Help clients build on successes. Instead of browbeating Anan (Counselor A), Counselor B reframes his studies and relating skills as two successful "jobs" and helps him present himself neither as a beggar nor by overselling.

8. Respect clients' values. Imposing values violates empowerment. Counselor A pushes a nursing home on a caregiving daughter; Counselor B invites her to explore what drives her priorities. Exploring values is not the same as questioning them.

Conclusion
Egan stresses that these are guidelines, not absolute prescriptions: helpers should use common sense, take the client's perspective and stay flexible. Box 7.1, "The Wisdom of Challenging", turns them into self-check questions, including ensuring self-challenge never becomes self-demeaning or self-destructive. Effective invitations thus depend as much on the helper's self-challenge as on technique.

practice.q: How should a helper manage client reluctance and resistance? Discuss with reference to Egan.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Egan distinguishes reluctance, the client's hesitancy to do the hard work of change, from resistance, the client's pushing back against perceived coercion or mistreatment. Both are pervasive, so managing them is part of all helping (Kottler). Egan's guidance has two parts: avoiding unhelpful responses and developing productive approaches.

Avoiding unhelpful responses
Beginners often feel panic, irritation, guilt or rejection and react with "fight or flight": placating, hostility, doing nothing, half-hearted work, trying to win the client by love, power struggles, being scapegoated, lowering expectations, handing over direction or giving up. These are fuelled by unspoken assumptions such as "every client must like me", "every unwilling client can (or cannot) be helped", "I alone am responsible" and "I must succeed with everyone". Effective helpers neither court nor are surprised by reluctance and resistance.

Productive approaches
1. Explore your own reluctance and resistance: how you react to coercion or unfairness and avoid growth.
2. See some reluctance and resistance as normal, even a sign of fibre and self-affirmation.
3. Accept and work with it. Teyber speaks of "honoring" resistance. Start from the client's frame of reference, share how you experience it, use immediacy, explore your own negative feelings, avoid moralizing and befriend it.
4. See reluctance as avoidance, not ill will (Watson & Tharp). If clients find counselling unrewarding, help them find incentives and talk about outcomes.
5. Examine the quality of your interventions: are you too directive or unfair? Own your emotions and do not overpersonalize; pressure may come from others.
6. Be realistic and flexible; rigid expectations create adversarial relationships.
7. Establish a "two-person just society" (Smaby & Tamminen) through mutual respect, shared planning and a jointly built contract.
8. Help the client search for incentives using self-interest and brainstorming, such as staying in charge of one's life.
9. Do not see yourself as the only helper; involve peers and family, as with lawyers in AA.
10. Employ reluctant and resistant clients as helpers, including role reversal; a resistant alcoholic joined AA after a week accompanying a member on his rounds.
Hanna, Hanna and Keys add 50 strategies grouped as reaching, accepting and relating.

In the moment, when a client reacts angrily to a tentative summary, Helper A's judicial "let's go through the evidence" invites argument, whereas Helper B backs off, reflects the client's feeling and gives space without retracting. Egan also notes Wessler, Hankin and Stern's warning that "difficult client" often signals the helper's own difficulty, while recognizing that clients' behaviour may reflect poor self-management.

Conclusion
Managing reluctance and resistance requires self-awareness, acceptance, collaboration and creativity rather than force. Resistance can even be healthy, opening collaborative decision making (Koenig). Helpers should rely on the values of Part I and the skills of Part II with clients who at first do not want help.

practice.q: Describe the shadow side of helpers with special reference to the MUM effect and the excuses helpers make for not challenging.
practice.answer:
Introduction
Helpers are human and have flaws and blind spots. Kottler's literature on helpers' humanity is valuable to beginners, since prevention is better than cure, and to veterans, who can still learn. Egan applies this to challenge: some helpers fail to invite clients to challenge themselves for reasons rooted in their own fears.

Identifying blind spots
Supervisors have a critical duty to help counsellors identify blind spots. After training, skilled helpers ask themselves "What am I missing here?", consult colleagues, scrutinize their role without becoming self-obsessed and keep learning about themselves, clients and the profession. Eliciting honest client feedback is one direct method.

The MUM effect
Rosen and Tesser described the MUM effect: the tendency to keep mum about undesirable messages and withhold bad news even when it is in the other's interest. Egan recalls that bearers of bad news to kings were sometimes killed. Invitations to self-challenge carry a kind of bad news and often arouse negative feelings in the challenger regardless of the receiver's likely reaction. Helpers comfortable with support but uneasy with helping as social influence can fall victim to it and become less effective.

Excuses for not challenging
Egan regards reluctance to challenge as a better starting point than eagerness, but stresses that all helping, even the most client-centred, involves social influence, so helpers must challenge themselves about challenging. Trainees discover assumptions such as: I am used to live-and-let-live and dislike intruding; if I challenge others I will be challenged and hurt; I may enjoy challenging and release hidden anger; I may hurt clients, as heavy-handed confrontation does; I may uncover problems I cannot handle; and clients will stop liking me. These persist into practice and affect human-service workers and managers who avoid giving feedback. Willingness to challenge also differs from the skill and wisdom to do so.

Box 7.2
Egan's self-check asks whether helpers can spot clients' games without cynicism, accept the "intrusiveness" of social influence, include invitations without becoming confrontation specialists, develop assertiveness to overcome the MUM effect, challenge their own excuses, and face their imperfections and blind spots as helpers and private citizens.

Links to the rest of the chapter
The shadow side connects with Egan's earlier guidelines. Berenson and Mitchell's demand that helpers earn the right to challenge, by being open to challenge themselves and working on their own lives, is itself a remedy for blind spots. Likewise, the self-defeating assumptions helpers bring to reluctant and resistant clients (for example, that every client must like them, or that they are consultants rather than social influencers) mirror the trainee excuses above. A helper who needs to be liked will both avoid challenging and react poorly when clients push back.

Conclusion
The shadow side reminds helpers that effective challenging begins with self-challenge. Egan's position is balanced: hesitancy about challenging is healthier than eagerness, but avoiding challenge altogether leaves helping bland and ineffective. Recognizing the MUM effect and one's excuses allows helpers to combine support with appropriate influence and to keep learning about themselves throughout their careers.

practice.q: Discuss the causes of resistance and explain the issue of involuntary clients.
practice.answer:
Introduction
For Egan, resistance is the client's reaction to coercion. Clients who resist believe they are being forced to do something; they may even want help but feel the helper demands rather than invites. Karl refused Laura's feedback surveys because he felt told what to do, though she intended no imposition.

Perceived mistreatment
Clients who feel mistreated, or feel their cultural beliefs, values and norms are violated, tend to resist; resistance is their way of fighting back (Dimond et al.; Driscoll). Spouses pressured into marriage counselling, like Tony who sees a "conspiracy" between his wife and her mother, resist what they see as a power play. Because people act on perceptions, even imagined coercion produces open or covert fighting back. Resistant clients deny needing help, avoid a working relationship, try to con counsellors, sabotage, terminate early or become belligerent, though in varying degrees.

Involuntary clients
Involuntary or "mandated" clients (Brodsky) are often resisters: a student sent to the counsellor as punishment, a felon on probation, a manager facing harassment charges. They are found in schools, correctional settings, court-mandated marriage counselling, employment and welfare agencies and court-related settings. Kiracofe and Wells object to disciplinary counselling in schools on professional and ethical grounds because it moves responsibility for change from the student to the counselling process; they propose readiness-based strategies aligned with Prochaska and call for a systemic solution.

Other resistant clients
Egan lists those who see no reason for help; resent referrers; fear the unknown; have a history of rebelliousness; see the system's goals as different from theirs; distrust "shrinks"; equate help with weakness and resist to save face; feel counselling is done to them; seek power by resisting authority; dislike the helper silently; disagree on how much change is needed; or differ greatly from the helper. Sociocultural variables such as gender, race, religion and class can also fuel resistance.

Healthy resistance
Resistance can be healthy: Koenig shows that it allows collaborative co-construction of acceptable recommendations, making clients agents.

Resistance versus reluctance
Resistance should be distinguished from reluctance. Reluctance has its seeds in the client and reflects hesitancy to do the hard work of change, arising from fear of intensity, lack of trust, fear of disorganization, shame, the cost of change or loss of hope. Resistance, by contrast, is a reaction to perceived pressure from outside. In practice the two are often mixed in the same client.

Implications for the helper
Because resistance is a reaction to coercion, the helper should examine whether his or her own behaviour seems unfair or too directive, deal with feelings of coercion by building a "two-person just society" based on mutual respect and shared planning, involve clients in all decisions and help them find incentives, such as remaining in charge of their own lives.

Conclusion
Resistance arises from perceived coercion and mismatch, not just client stubbornness. The helper's job is to spot it and work with the client to find its cause rather than meet it with hostility.

summary: Self-challenge applies to helpers too; professions evolve, so helpers must keep updating their practice (p. 192).
Invitations must be wise as well as accurate: based on understanding, caring, genuine, promoting self-responsibility and action (p. 192).
Eight guidelines: keep goals in mind, provide choice structure, earn the right, be specific, be tentative not apologetic, challenge strengths, build on successes, respect values (pp. 192–199).
Berenson and Mitchell: helpers earn the right to challenge through relationship, empathy, openness to challenge and working on their own lives (p. 194).
Challenge unused strengths, not weaknesses; even adversity can yield benefits (p. 196).
Reluctance = hesitancy to do the work of change (seeds in the client); resistance = pushing back against perceived coercion (pp. 199, 202).
Reasons for reluctance: fear of intensity, lack of trust, fear of disorganization, shame, cost of change, loss of hope (pp. 200–202).
Involuntary (mandated) clients and many others who feel coerced, mistreated or different from the helper often resist; resistance can also be healthy (pp. 203–204).
Avoid 'fight or flight' responses and self-defeating assumptions such as 'every client must like me' (p. 205).

Productive approaches: explore your own resistance, see it as normal, honor it, see reluctance as avoidance, examine your interventions, be flexible, build a 'two-person just society', find incentives, involve others, use clients as helpers (pp. 205–207).
When clients react defensively, back off and give space rather than argue; 'difficult client' often reflects the helper's difficulty (pp. 207–208).
Principled negotiation (Fisher, Ury & Patton) values fairness: avoid rigid positions, separate people from issues, focus on interests, mutual options, objective criteria (pp. 209–211).
Counsellors can help clients negotiate with others and with themselves, as with Mara's cultural selves (p. 211).
Shadow side: helpers must find blind spots via supervision, colleagues and client feedback (p. 211).
The MUM effect and trainees' excuses lead helpers to avoid challenge; all helping involves social influence (pp. 212–213).
